headline: Amazon describes itself as a customer-obsessed builder of scale, emphasizing leadership principles and diversity language that peaked around 2017.
identity: Amazon has consistently valued customer obsession, innovation, and high performance standards across its careers messaging. The company leaned heavily into diversity and inclusion language from 2016–2018 (explicit demographic mentions peaked at 25 in 2018), then substantially reduced that emphasis by 2019 onward, shifting toward vaguer aspirational framing. AI and machine learning appeared sporadically (2018–2021) but have been absent from the copy since 2021, despite the company's public investments in those areas.
fit: You might be a good fit if you are driven by customer impact, comfortable with high performance bars, and energized by technical problem-solving. The company's language reaches for builders, inventors, and people who thrive in fast-moving environments—but less so for those seeking explicit commitments to belonging or community-focused work.

sections.heading: The Rise and Retreat of Diversity Language
sections.body: Amazon's careers copy embraced explicit diversity messaging most aggressively from 2016 to 2018. In 2017, the company mentioned specific affinity groups (Black Employee Network, Latinos@Amazon, Amazon Women in Engineering), discussed pay equity, and featured employee stories centered on underrepresented backgrounds. By 2018, 25 chunks contained explicit demographic references. However, this emphasis contracted sharply: 2019 saw only 1 explicit demographic mention, and by 2023–2024, the company reverted to vaguer language like "we strive to reflect the diversity of our customers" without naming specific groups or commitments. The inclusion score (a measure of how welcoming the language feels) peaked in 2017 at 0.6152 and has remained lower since 2019 (averaging ~0.38).

sections.heading: Leadership Principles and Performance Over Belonging
sections.body: Throughout the period, Amazon's core messaging centered on its Leadership Principles—customer obsession, ownership, bias for action, frugality, and high hiring bars. The craft axis (quality of work and craftsmanship) spiked in 2007 (zscore 1.96) and again in 2016 (1.87), reflecting detailed articulation of what excellence looks like. By contrast, altruism language (community benefit, social good) peaked in 2017 (zscore 1.60) but has since declined. The company's wellbeing messaging remained muted until 2023–2026, when it began emphasizing benefits, safety, and upskilling—suggesting a shift toward tangible employee value propositions rather than cultural belonging.

sections.heading: Absent AI, Persistent Innovation Framing
sections.body: Despite Amazon's major investments in Alexa, machine learning, and AWS, AI language appeared in only 4 years of careers copy (2018, 2019, 2021) and has been entirely absent since. When it did appear, it was confined to employee stories about Alexa and computer vision work. Techno-optimism language (celebrating technological progress) peaked in 2011 and 2013 but has been minimal since 2019. Instead, the company frames itself through innovation and invention as cultural values—"invent and simplify," "we pioneer"—rather than as a place to work on cutting-edge AI. This gap between public narrative and careers messaging is notable.
